title: Why Toddlers Have Tantrums
hook: Tantrums are a normal part of toddler development — big feelings hitting a brain that can't yet manage them or fully put them into words.

title: Reading Together: Start at Birth
hook: You don't need to wait until your child can follow a story. Reading aloud from birth builds language, attention, and your bond — and even a few interactive minutes a day counts.

title: You Can't Pour From an Empty Cup
hook: Looking after yourself isn't a luxury — it's part of caring for your baby. A rested, supported parent has more patience and presence to give.

title: Healing After Birth Takes Weeks, Not Days
hook: Your body just did something huge, and recovery is a season, not a single appointment. Bleeding, cramps, healing, and mood shifts are all part of the fourth trimester.

title: Feeding on Demand: Cues and How Often
hook: Newborns feed best on demand — watch for early hunger cues rather than the clock, and let wet and dirty diapers, not the exact count of feeds, reassure you they're getting enough.

title: Newborn Jaundice: Common and Usually Harmless
hook: Many newborns turn a little yellow in the first days — jaundice is common, usually harmless, and often clears on its own, but a few warning signs mean get it checked promptly.

title: Tummy Time: Back to Sleep, Tummy to Play
hook: The same babies who must sleep on their backs need time on their tummies while awake — it builds the strength behind rolling and crawling, and helps keep the back of the head from flattening.

title: Choking and Infant CPR
hook: Most choking is preventable with the right food sizes and small objects kept away — and infants get a different response than adults: back blows and chest thrusts, never abdominal thrusts.

title: The Routine Tests and Shot of the First Days
hook: In the first days, a healthy newborn gets a heel-prick blood screen, a hearing check, a heart-oxygen check, and a vitamin K shot — quick, routine steps that catch rare but serious problems early.

title: Folic Acid Before and During Pregnancy
hook: Taking folic acid before conception and in early pregnancy is one of the best-evidenced ways to lower the risk of serious birth defects of the brain and spine.

title: The Common Cold in Children
hook: Young kids catch a lot of colds — that's normal. Colds are viral, so antibiotics won't help; comfort care does, and OTC cough-and-cold medicines aren't safe for little ones.

title: Childproofing the Home
hook: Anchoring furniture and TVs is the childproofing step parents skip most — and tip-overs are one of the deadliest home hazards for young kids. Then you cover the rest and redo it as baby gets mobile.

title: Car Seat Safety
hook: The car seat protects best when three things line up: rear-facing for as long as the seat allows, a harness snug enough you can't pinch the strap, and the back seat.

title: The Toddler Language Explosion
hook: Somewhere in the second year, many toddlers go from a handful of words to picking up new ones almost daily — and talking with them is what fuels it.

title: Eating Well When You're Pregnant
hook: Most foods are fine in pregnancy — but a short list carries infection or toxin risks worth knowing, alongside a daily folic acid supplement and a varied, balanced diet.

title: Developmental Milestones: The Big Picture
hook: Development happens across several areas at once — social, language, thinking, and movement — and milestones describe what most kids do by an age, not deadlines every child must hit.

title: Helping Kids Manage Big Feelings
hook: Young children can't yet calm themselves down on their own — they borrow your calm. Naming feelings and co-regulating now builds the self-regulation that grows with age.

title: Motor Milestones: Rolling to Crawling
hook: In the first year babies move through a rough sequence — rolling, sitting, crawling, pulling to stand — but the timing varies widely, and ranges matter more than exact dates.

title: Caring for the First Teeth
hook: Baby teeth matter — they hold space for adult teeth and shape eating and speech. Brushing starts with the very first tooth, and the first dental visit comes earlier than most parents expect.

title: Foods to Skip Before Baby's First Birthday
hook: A few foods are genuinely risky for babies under one — honey can cause botulism, cow's milk shouldn't be the main drink yet, and round, hard foods are choking hazards.

title: What Newborn Sleep Really Looks Like
hook: Newborns sleep a lot — but in short bursts, with no day-night rhythm yet. Frequent night waking to feed is normal and expected, not a problem to fix.

title: Spit-Up vs. Reflux: When It's Just Laundry
hook: Most babies spit up — it's a plumbing issue, not an illness, and a happy, growing 'spitter' needs patience, not treatment. A few specific signs are the ones worth a doctor's call.

title: Fever Basics for Parents
hook: A fever is a sign the body is fighting infection, not a disease itself — how your child looks and acts often matters more than the exact number on the thermometer.

title: The Common Aches of Pregnancy
hook: Nausea, heartburn, fatigue, and a sore back are the everyday companions of pregnancy — usually normal and manageable. The skill is knowing the simple fixes, and which symptoms are not on this list.

title: Well-Child Visits: Your Regular Check-Ups
hook: Well-child visits aren't just for when something's wrong — they track growth and development, deliver vaccines on schedule, and catch problems early, even when your child seems perfectly fine.

title: Vaccines That Protect You and Your Baby
hook: Certain vaccines in pregnancy do double duty: they protect you from serious illness and pass antibodies to your baby, shielding them in the early weeks before their own shots.

title: Toddler Sleep: Routines and Naps
hook: Toddlers (1–2 years) typically need 11–14 hours of sleep per 24 hours, naps included. A predictable bedtime routine does more for sleep than almost anything else.

title: Poison and Medicine Safety
hook: Most poisonings happen with a parent home but distracted. Store medicines and cleaners locked, up, and in their original containers — and save Poison Control: 1-800-222-1222.

title: Vomiting and Dehydration
hook: When a stomach bug hits, the real risk isn't the vomiting itself — it's dehydration. The goal is keeping fluids in with small, frequent sips, and knowing the signs that mean call the doctor.

title: Serve and Return: Talking Builds the Brain
hook: Every time you answer your baby's coo, babble, or gesture, you're building their brain. These back-and-forth 'serve and return' moments are the engine of early language — and they're free.

title: Play Is How Young Children Learn
hook: For young children, play isn't a break from learning — it is the learning, building language, problem-solving, and social skills all at once.

title: Picky Eating Is Normal
hook: Picky eating is a normal toddler stage, not a battle to win. The reliable approach: you decide what and when to offer, your child decides whether and how much to eat.

title: Stranger Anxiety: A New Kind of Wary
hook: Around 6 to 9 months, a once-sociable baby may suddenly turn shy or cry around unfamiliar people — even doting grandparents. It's a normal sign their mind and memory are growing.

title: Preparing Formula Safely
hook: Powdered formula isn't sterile, so safe prep is about hygiene and getting the ratio exactly right — clean hands and equipment, the correct water-to-powder mix, and fresh feeds made one at a time.

title: Crying Is a Newborn's Main Language
hook: Crying is how a newborn communicates every need — and a lot of crying in the first months is normal, peaking around six weeks and easing after that.

title: How Kids Learn to Make Friends
hook: Sharing and taking turns aren't automatic — they develop gradually through play. Preschoolers grow real social skills with practice, and adults coach by modeling and naming.

title: Soothing a Fussy Newborn
hook: Newborns are wired to be calmed by sensations that echo the womb — holding, swaddling, gentle motion, white noise, and sucking. One rule overrides all: never, ever shake a baby.

title: Growth Charts: Why the Curve Beats the Number
hook: A percentile compares your child to other kids the same age and sex — it's not a grade. The 10th is no better or worse than the 90th; what matters is the trend along your child's own curve.

title: Pumping and Storing Breast Milk
hook: Expressing milk lets someone else share feeds and keeps supply going when you're back at work. The trick is a simple storage rule — and gentle handling so the milk stays good for baby.

title: How Childhood Vaccines Work
hook: Vaccines train a child's immune system to recognize a disease in advance, so it can fight off the real thing — and they're scheduled to protect kids when they're most vulnerable.

title: What School Readiness Really Means
hook: Being ready for school is less about reading early and more about social and emotional skills — following directions, taking turns, and managing feelings.

title: When to Call the Doctor — Red Flags
hook: Most childhood illnesses are mild, but a handful of signs mean don't wait and watch — get medical help right away. Knowing them takes the guesswork out of a scary moment.

title: Water Safety
hook: Drowning is fast and silent — no splashing, no shouting. The single best protection for a young child is an adult within arm's reach whenever there's water.

title: Why Prenatal Visits Matter
hook: Regular checkups during pregnancy catch problems early — for many a typical schedule is monthly, then every two weeks, then weekly as the due date nears.

title: A Smoke-Free World Is Safer for Babies
hook: Keeping a baby away from smoke is one of the few SIDS risk factors parents fully control — and it also means fewer chest infections, ear infections, and asthma flare-ups.

title: Positive Discipline: Teaching, Not Punishing
hook: Discipline means teaching, not hurting. The AAP's most effective tools are calm consistency, catching good behavior, and clear consequences — and it advises against spanking and harsh words.

title: When Good Sleep Suddenly Gets Worse
hook: Sleep that was going well can fall apart around growth spurts, teething, travel, or illness. These rough patches are normal, they pass, and a steady routine helps you ride them out.

title: Separation Anxiety: A Sign of a Strong Bond
hook: When your baby melts down the moment you leave, it's not a setback — it's a normal phase and a sign of healthy attachment. Brief, confident goodbyes and a consistent ritual help.

title: Choosing Child Care You Trust
hook: Picking who cares for your child is a big decision. The main thing to look for is quality: small groups, low ratios, safety, and warm, steady caregivers.

title: Croup and Noisy Breathing
hook: Croup's barky, seal-like cough can be alarming at 2 a.m., but most cases are mild and viral. Knowing how to calm your child — and the breathing signs that mean emergency — makes all the difference.

title: Why Breastfed Babies Need Vitamin D Drops
hook: Breast milk is nearly perfect — but it's low in vitamin D. Pediatricians recommend a daily 400 IU vitamin D supplement for every breastfed and partly breastfed baby, starting in the first days.

title: Potty Training: Readiness Over Age
hook: There's no magic age to potty train. Readiness signs matter far more — and a calm, child-led, pressure-free approach beats pushing a child who isn't ready yet.

title: Starting Solid Foods
hook: Most babies are ready for their first solid foods at around six months — alongside continued breast milk or formula, not instead of it.

title: Why Outdoor Play Punches Above Its Weight
hook: Time outside does more than burn energy. It builds strong bodies, sharper focus, braver problem-solvers — and a growing body of research links it to healthier eyesight.

title: What Play Looks Like at Each Age
hook: Play is a child's real work — and it changes shape as they grow, from staring at your face to elaborate make-believe. The best 'toy' is usually a tuned-in grown-up, not a gadget.

title: Always Put a Baby to Sleep on Their Back
hook: Placing healthy babies on their back for every sleep — naps and night — is the single most effective step to reduce the risk of sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS).

title: A Safe Sleep Space for Baby
hook: Pediatric guidance for safer infant sleep is simple: a firm, flat surface with nothing in it — no pillows, blankets, bumpers, or soft toys.

title: Screen Time for Little Kids: Less, Together, On Purpose
hook: For babies under about 18 months the AAP says skip screens except video chat. For toddlers and preschoolers, keep it limited and high-quality, watch together, and protect sleep, meals, and play.

title: Your Relationship After Baby
hook: A new baby tests even strong relationships. Sharing the load, talking honestly, and working as a team — while expecting routines and intimacy to shift for a while — helps you weather it together.

title: Sleep Training, Without the Dogma
hook: There's no single 'right' way to help a baby sleep. Readiness is usually around 4–6 months, methods range from gradual check-ins to gentler approaches, and consistency matters most.

title: Breastfeeding: Getting Off to a Good Start
hook: A deep latch is the foundation of comfortable, effective breastfeeding — and most early hurdles like soreness and engorgement settle once attachment and supply find their rhythm.

title: How You'll Know Labour Has Started
hook: Labour usually announces itself with regular, strengthening contractions — sometimes alongside a 'show' or your waters breaking — and then unfolds in three broad stages.

title: Developmental Delays: Trust Your Gut, Don't Wait and See
hook: If something about your child's development worries you, say so early. Routine screening and prompt action — not waiting and seeing — give kids the best shot, because early intervention helps.

title: Baby Blues or Something More?
hook: Weepy and overwhelmed in the first days is common and usually passes within two weeks. When low mood lingers and disrupts daily life, it may be postpartum depression — common and treatable.

title: Sun Safety: Shade First for the Littlest
hook: Baby skin burns fast and shows damage for life. Under 6 months the rule is shade and clothing, not sunscreen; after that, sunscreen joins the hat and shade — not replaces them.

title: Teething: Signs and Safe Soothing
hook: Teething often starts around 6 months, but the timing varies a lot. Expect drooling, gum-rubbing, and fussiness — not a high fever, which points to something else.

title: Common Rashes in Babies and Kids
hook: Most childhood rashes — diaper rash, eczema, heat rash, hand-foot-and-mouth — are common and harmless. There's one big exception worth memorizing: a rash that doesn't fade when you press it.

title: Caring for the Umbilical Cord Stump
hook: The cord stump needs almost nothing — just keep it clean and dry and let it fall off on its own, usually within about three weeks. A few signs, though, mean call the doctor.

title: Ear Infections in Young Children
hook: Ear infections are one of the most common reasons little kids see the doctor — and many clear up on their own, which is why doctors often watch and wait before reaching for antibiotics.

title: When Toddlers Bite and Hit
hook: Biting and hitting horrify parents, but in toddlers they're rarely about meanness — they're big feelings meeting small vocabularies. Calm, consistent responses work better than punishment.

title: Warning Signs That Can't Wait
hook: Serious complications can happen during pregnancy and for up to a year after birth. Knowing the urgent warning signs — and insisting on being heard — can save a life.

title: New Baby, Older Sibling: Easing the Transition
hook: A new baby is a big change for an older child. Prepare them ahead, expect some jealousy and regression, protect one-on-one time, skip comparisons, and coach them through the rough patches.

title: Pregnancy Symptoms to Never Ignore
hook: A few symptoms in pregnancy mean call your midwife or maternity unit straight away — they can signal serious problems like pre-eclampsia that need checking without delay.

title: How Language Unfolds — and When to Check
hook: Understanding always runs ahead of talking. Knowing the rough order of language milestones — and the handful of red flags — helps you tell normal variation from a delay worth acting on.

title: Breastfeeding and Formula Both Feed a Baby Well
hook: Health bodies recommend breastfeeding where possible, but properly prepared infant formula is a safe, nourishing alternative — a fed baby is the goal.
